section_1.title: Prerequisite Recap: The 'Same-Dimension' Rule
section_1.content: Briefly review how square matrices (e.g., 2x2) transform space while staying in the same dimension. Establish the 'Grid' visual: basis vectors i-hat and j-hat moving but remaining on a 2D plane.
section_1.example: A 2x2 matrix rotating a 2D drawing of a 'Flatland Cat' 45 degrees while keeping it on the screen.

section_2.title: The Tall Matrix: Elevating to 3D (2x3 Transform)
section_2.content: Introduce the 3x2 matrix. Explain that it takes 2 input coordinates and outputs 3 coordinates. Geometrically, this maps a 2D plane into a 3D space. The columns represent where the original 2D basis vectors land in the 3D world.
section_2.example: A 3x2 matrix lifting a 2D 'Paper Mario' character off a flat page and placing him as a slanted sheet floating in a 3D room.

section_3.title: The Wide Matrix: The Great Squish (3x2 Transform)
section_3.content: Introduce the 2x3 matrix. This takes a 3D vector and maps it onto a 2D plane. Explain 'Dimensionality Reduction'—how information is lost when we project high-dimensional objects into lower-dimensional spaces.
section_3.example: A 3D 'Low-poly Bird' flying in the air, while a 2x3 matrix calculates its 2D shadow cast on the flat ground. The depth information disappears.

section_4.title: The Rule of Rows and Columns
section_4.content: A visual mnemonic for matrix dimensions (m x n). The 'n' (columns) is the dimension of the space we start in (the number of input basis vectors). The 'm' (rows) is the dimension of the space we land in.
section_4.example: A 'Magic Portal' analogy: If the portal has 3 input slots but only 2 output wires, the 3D input must be squashed to exit.

section_5.title: Column Space: The Footprint of the Transformation
section_5.content: Explain that even if a matrix maps to 3D space (3x2), the result is restricted to the span of its columns. This 'Column Space' is the only area in the target dimension that the transformation can reach.
section_5.example: A 3x2 matrix creates a 2D 'Glass Pane' floating in a 3D aquarium; the fish (vectors) can only exist on that specific pane, not the whole tank.

section_6.title: Summary & Application
section_6.content: Synthesize the concept: Non-square matrices are 'Inter-dimensional Bridges.' Mention real-world applications like Computer Vision (projecting 3D scenes onto 2D screens).
section_6.example: A camera lens acting as a wide matrix, compressing a 3D mountain range into a 2D digital photo.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section6Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title = "Summary & Application"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Non-square matrices act as bridges between different dimensions.",
            "Cameras project 3D worlds onto 2D digital sensors.",
            "Linear algebra powers these inter-dimensional transformations."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_BRIDGE = BLUE_C
        COLOR_MOUNTAIN = "#00FF00"

section_1.content: Briefly review how square matrices (e.g., 2x2) transform space while staying in the same dimension. Establish the 'Grid' visual: basis vectors i-hat and j-hat moving but remaining on a 2D plane.
section_1.example: A 2x2 matrix rotating a 2D drawing of a 'Flatland Cat' 45 degrees while keeping it on the screen.

section_2.title: The Tall Matrix: Elevating to 3D (2x3 Transform)
section_2.content: Introduce the 3x2 matrix. Explain that it takes 2 input coordinates and outputs 3 coordinates. Geometrically, this maps a 2D plane into a 3D space. The columns represent where the original 2D basis vectors land in the 3D world.
section_2.example: A 3x2 matrix lifting a 2D 'Paper Mario' character off a flat page and placing him as a slanted sheet floating in a 3D room.

section_3.title: The Wide Matrix: The Great Squish (3x2 Transform)
section_3.content: Introduce the 2x3 matrix. This takes a 3D vector and maps it onto a 2D plane. Explain 'Dimensionality Reduction'—how information is lost when we project high-dimensional objects into lower-dimensional spaces.
section_3.example: A 3D 'Low-poly Bird' flying in the air, while a 2x3 matrix calculates its 2D shadow cast on the flat ground. The depth information disappears.

section_4.title: The Rule of Rows and Columns
section_4.content: A visual mnemonic for matrix dimensions (m x n). The 'n' (columns) is the dimension of the space we start in (the number of input basis vectors). The 'm' (rows) is the dimension of the space we land in.

section_5.title: Column Space: The Footprint of the Transformation
section_5.content: Explain that even if a matrix maps to 3D space (3x2), the result is restricted to the span of its columns. This 'Column Space' is the only area in the target dimension that the transformation can reach.
section_5.example: A 3x2 matrix creates a 2D 'Glass Pane' floating in a 3D aquarium; the fish (vectors) can only exist on that specific pane, not the whole tank.

        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"

        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):

        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        # Group vectors with labels for coordinated movement/rotation

        )
        self.place_at_grid(matrix, 'A3', scale_factor=0.9)
        
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.play(Write(matrix))
        self.wait(1)

        self.play(

        )

import numpy as np

# Use the provided TeachingScene base class without modification.
class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)

        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom

            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):

        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # 1. Setup layout
        title_text = "Prerequisite Recap: The 'Same-Dimension' Rule"
        lecture_lines = [
            "- Square matrices transform space while keeping its dimension.",
            "- A 2x2 matrix moves vectors within the 2D plane.",
            "- Basis vectors i-hat and j-hat shift but stay flat."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # 2. Prepare Visual Elements
        # Plane
        plane = NumberPlane(
            x_range=[-2, 2, 1],
            y_range=[-2, 2, 1],
            x_length=4,
            y_length=4,
            background_line_style={
                "stroke_color": BLUE_D,
                "stroke_width": 2,
                "stroke_opacity": 0.3
            }
        )
        
        # Simple Cat Illustration (Flatland Cat)
        cat_color = "#F0E68C" # Khaki
        body = Ellipse(width=0.6, height=0.4, color=cat_color, fill_opacity=1)
        head = Circle(radius=0.25, color=cat_color, fill_opacity=1).move_to(body.get_left() + UP*0.1)
        ear_l = Triangle(color=cat_color, fill_opacity=1).scale(0.1).rotate(30*DEGREES).move_to(head.get_top() + LEFT*0.1)
        ear_r = Triangle(color=cat_color, fill_opacity=1).scale(0.1).rotate(-30*DEGREES).move_to(head.get_top() + RIGHT*0.1)
        cat = VGroup(body, head, ear_l, ear_r)
        
        # Basis Vectors and Labels
        i_hat = Vector([1, 0], color="#FF0000") # red i-hat
        j_hat = Vector([0, 1], color="#00FF00") # green j-hat
        i_label = MathTex(r"\hat{i}", color="#FF0000", font_size=24)
        j_label = MathTex(r"\hat{j}", color="#00FF00", font_size=24)
        
        # Group vectors with labels for coordinated movement/rotation
        i_group = VGroup(i_hat, i_label)
        j_group = VGroup(j_hat, j_label)
        
        # Initial relative positioning (standard positions)
        i_label.next_to(i_hat, RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        j_label.next_to(j_hat, UP, buff=0.1)
        
        # Main visual group (Plane + Cat + Vectors)
        # We group them so they transform together as one "space"
        visual_group = VGroup(plane, cat, i_group, j_group)
        
        # Use grid system for positioning the entire coordinate system
        # Placed in the right-side area
        self.place_in_area(visual_group, 'B2', 'F5', scale_factor=0.8)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Line 1: Square matrices transform space while keeping its dimension.
        # Action: Fade in grid and the flatland cat.
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(FadeIn(plane), Create(cat), run_time=2)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Line 2: A 2x2 matrix moves vectors within the 2D plane.
        # Action: Display the 2x2 rotation matrix at the top of the grid area.
        matrix = MathTex(
            r"R = \begin{bmatrix} \cos 45^\circ & -\sin 45^\circ \\ \sin 45^\circ & \cos 45^\circ \end{bmatrix}",
            color=WHITE, font_size=32
        )
        self.place_at_grid(matrix, 'A3', scale_factor=0.9)
        
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.play(Write(matrix))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Line 3: Basis vectors i-hat and j-hat shift but stay flat.
        # Action: Introduce basis vectors, then rotate the whole space.
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        self.play(
            GrowArrow(i_hat),
            FadeIn(i_label),
            GrowArrow(j_hat),
            FadeIn(j_label),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)
        
        # Transformation: Rotate the entire space (grid + cat + vectors) 45 degrees CCW
        # about_point=plane.get_center() ensures rotation around the coordinate origin
        self.play(
            Rotate(visual_group, angle=45*DEGREES, about_point=plane.get_center()),
            run_time=3
        )
        self.wait(2)

        # Transformation matrix to simulate a 3D isometric slant

            run_time=2,

        )
